coverageNote: Read all 41 current Markdown sources in scope, including the two domain-level index/CX files as shared context; completed 3a implementer simulation, 3b Vision-Rubric scoring, and 3c devil's-advocate probing for every file. The seven units are 20.01 through 20.07; 8 rubric dimensions × 7 units = 56 applicable checkpoints.

findings.claim: The 20.01 unresolved-question register names an owner and a deferred stage but supplies neither of the required fields: a deadline and the decision blocked.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
Q-04 asks for the retention period and queued-observation review SLA, but records only owners and deferred stages.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when retention and resolver-SLA decisions become mandatory and which implementation decision may proceed in the meantime.
findings.failureScenario: A slice ships with an arbitrary retention period or no manual-review backstop for unresolved identities because the question never becomes due or blocks a release.

findings.claim: Imported weak-provenance records have no resolved send-eligibility policy, and the legality of the only proposed re-permission path remains unresolved.

evidence.excerpt: Whether weak-provenance records are sendable-with-warning or hard-blocked until re-permissioned is marked PENDING.
Whether a re-permission campaign to imported records is lawful is marked PENDING and needs counsel.
The 200k-row stale-list case leaves whether stale consent blocks sending as PENDING.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose a contactability state and whether a platform may send a re-permission message to an imported address.
findings.failureScenario: A stale or purchased list is contacted without a lawful basis, causing recipient harm and shared-sender complaint or blocklist damage.

findings.claim: The 20.02 unresolved-question register has owners and deferred stages, but no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
Q-03 says cross-entity segments directly contradict per-entity records and must resolve before either ships, but gives no deadline or blocked-decision field.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when cross-entity segmentation must be decided and whether tenant-isolation work may proceed.
findings.failureScenario: One implementation assumes cross-entity joins while another enforces isolated records, producing an authorization and data-visibility conflict.

findings.claim: The specification identifies individual-targeting through segments as a stalking hazard but does not define the send/export k-anonymity constraint or its enforcement boundary.

evidence.excerpt: The one-person segment case leaves whether a k-anonymity floor applies to sends as PENDING.
DT-03 calls the hazard real, proposes a floor on send/export, and states that the author is not confident enough to decide it.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose whether a one-person segment can be sent or exported and select the minimum audience threshold and exception rules.
findings.failureScenario: A manager or artist uses demographic and location filters to target or export information about an identifiable fan.

findings.claim: Perk redemption is acknowledged as a score-ratcheting feedback loop, but no product policy determines whether it is excluded, down-weighted, or counterbalanced.

evidence.excerpt: Redemption raises the score, which grants the next perk and raises the score again; the ratchet is described as the default behavior.
The three mutually different redemption policies are marked PENDING for an owner ruling.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose the scoring treatment for redemption and whether perk inventory reserves exist.
findings.failureScenario: Early recipients become permanently top-tier through prior platform choices rather than current loyalty, making eligibility unfair and score outputs misleading.

findings.claim: The 20.03 unresolved-question register has owners and deferred stages, but no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
Q-01 leaves the shared-versus-per-artist sending-domain choice open without a deadline or a field naming the blocked architecture decision.
The domain-level copy of the sending-domain question also has only User and /create-prd-architecture.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when the sender-domain architecture must be locked and which messaging work is prohibited until then.
findings.failureScenario: Teams build incompatible shared-domain and per-artist-DNS assumptions, leaving onboarding, reputation isolation, and provider integration inconsistent.

findings.claim: The mid-send circuit breaker lacks numeric complaint thresholds and ramp curves, and the platform-wide blocklist response has no runbook.

evidence.excerpt: Thresholds, ramp curves, and the reputation model are marked PENDING.
The sending-domain blocklist incident is marked PENDING and requires an incident runbook.
A complaint spike must rate-drop or halt immediately, but no trigger value is specified.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must select complaint limits, ramp rates, halt behavior, recovery authority, and the incident response flow.
findings.failureScenario: A bad imported send continues long enough to damage the shared sending domain, while operators have no defined containment or recovery procedure.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
The no-rights-record policy states that its prior deferral expired, yet provides no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.
The domain-level no-rights-record question repeats owner and /create-prd only.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when unresolved commerce-policy choices become release blockers and whether interim defaults are allowed to ship.
findings.failureScenario: The catalogue launches under an unratified rights policy or a pricing/payout choice is silently locked by the first implementation.

findings.claim: The D2F payout flow requires financial-regulatory, tax, reserve, versioned-terms, and payee-assent decisions that remain unresolved.

evidence.excerpt: Whether held collaborator funds make the platform a money transmitter or e-money institution is open.
Tax collection, withholding, and reporting obligations for multi-party payouts remain open.
The versioned basis-terms record and payout-engine resolution are not modeled anywhere.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose a custody model, compliance gates, tax lifecycle, terms-version data model, and proof of a payee's assent.
findings.failureScenario: Funds are accumulated or paid under an unlicensed, tax-incomplete, or non-provable agreement model, exposing collaborators and the platform to financial loss and disputes.

findings.claim: The 20.05 unresolved-question register has owners and deferred stages, but no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
The fulfilment-milestone and verifier question names an owner but has no deadline or explicit decision blocked.
The domain-level money-transmission question also records only User and /create-prd-security.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when the custody, release, and fulfilment decisions must close and which campaign work they block.
findings.failureScenario: Crowdfunding implementation advances despite no enforceable release or custody decision, so product behavior is determined by an arbitrary engineering default.

findings.claim: The campaign fund-release lifecycle leaves custody, milestone verification, advance funding, insolvency protection, and partial-fulfilment refunds unresolved.

evidence.excerpt: The behavior calls who verifies a milestone an unsolved problem.
Whether the platform holds money and what happens on platform insolvency are explicitly unresolved.
Advance-tranche behavior is PENDING because the author declines to invent an answer.
First-come versus pro-rata refunds after partial fulfilment are PENDING.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent the escrow/custody actor, release authority and evidence, advance policy, insolvency protection, and allocation of an exhausted refund pool.
findings.failureScenario: Backer funds are released to a vanished or non-performing artist, become insolvent-estate assets, or are refunded unfairly after only some rewards ship.

findings.claim: The 20.06 unresolved-question register has owners and deferred stages, but no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
The anonymous-follow identity model is open but gives only User and /create-prd-security.
The conflicting alert-radius question gives only User and /create-prd.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when identity, consent, and radius decisions close and which alert flows remain blocked until then.
findings.failureScenario: Separate alert implementations make incompatible assumptions about fan identity, consent, and distance settings.

findings.claim: The gig-alert behavior still says web is the only surface while its resolved question says v1 includes a PWA with web push.

evidence.excerpt: The behavior describes the phone-shaped product and states that constraints declare web as the only surface.
Resolved Q-01 states that v1 is web plus PWA and PWA web push is the alert channel.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose whether v1 requires installable-PWA and push-subscription behavior or a web-only alert surface.
findings.failureScenario: The product ships without the stated PWA alert channel or teams build incompatible assumptions about push permissions, installation, and fallback delivery.

findings.claim: Anonymous follow is required to avoid an account wall, but the durable identity, later-account linking, and consent boundary are explicitly unspecified.

evidence.excerpt: The no-account follow case says it needs an anonymous-to-identified path and a durable contact point.
Q-01 says the unresolved model must determine the pre-identification key, later signup link, duplicate handling, and consent carried by email capture.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must invent an anonymous identifier, account-claim/link rules, email capture behavior, retention, and alert-consent semantics.
findings.failureScenario: Follows cannot reliably fire alerts after a device or account change, or captured contact data is linked and contacted without a defensible permission model.

findings.claim: The alert-radius value conflicts with the preference-centre radius, and the source does not resolve whether they are one setting or two.

evidence.excerpt: Gig alerts default to 25 miles / 40 km and permit widening to an unspecified maximum.
Q-05 identifies the 25-mile/40-km versus 50-mile/80-km and 10–500-km contradiction, with no owner ruling.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose a distance value, maximum, persistence location, and whether marketing and gig alerts read one preference or separate preferences.
findings.failureScenario: Fans configure one radius but receive or miss alerts according to a different radius, making notification behavior unpredictable.

findings.claim: The 20.07 unresolved-question register has owners and deferred stages, but no deadline or explicit decision-blocked field.

evidence.excerpt: | # | Question | Owner | Deferred To |
The public-versus-artist-only request decision is unresolved but has only User and /create-prd.
The k-anonymity threshold question has only User and /create-prd-security.

findings.forcedInvention: A delivery owner must invent when visibility and disclosure-safety decisions are due and which request/map surfaces they block.
findings.failureScenario: A fan-demand feature ships with unreviewed visibility or privacy defaults because no decision has a due date or explicit release dependency.

findings.claim: Fan-facing request visibility is internally unreconciled: the Role Lens grants fans visibility of others' requests, while the open question says the available scope is artist/promoter only.

evidence.excerpt: The Fan Role Lens says the fan asks for a show and sees others asking.
Q-01 calls the public-versus-artist-only choice unreconciled and notes that the other scope names no fan-visible count.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must choose request visibility, viewer authorization, aggregation, moderation, and anti-brigading behavior.
findings.failureScenario: The system exposes demand counts to fans when the intended access model is private, enabling brigading and misleading fans about artist commitment.

findings.claim: The demand map mandates a k-anonymity floor but does not define k or whether explicit requests receive the same protection.

evidence.excerpt: The sparse-region case requires a k-anonymity floor on the map but provides no threshold.
Q-05 says D-05 names no threshold and asks whether the floor covers explicit requests as well as passive density.

findings.forcedInvention: An implementer must select the disclosure threshold, geographic aggregation behavior, and whether request-board counts bypass the same protection.
findings.failureScenario: A map or request board reveals that a named small group of fans is in a sparse region, exposing their location and interest to an artist or operator.
